text: The Wall of Busan's first shift back lasts one stroke of a ladle, and the crawler turns to ash.
Her slippers haven't moved an inch.
Jaeha stares up at her, his bleeding arm forgotten.
Two more crawlers surge out. She backhands one and stamps on the other.
But Jaeha is watching the ring of force spreading off the ladle.
He knows that wasn't a hard hit. Geum, wiping the ladle, has another word for it.
The sea is getting bolder, she says. When he begs once more about that man, she gives in.
They sit on the parapet, Nib on watch.
The colour drains, and the sea turns violet: the night the gates opened.
The sea boils, boats burn, and at the breakwater's neck, fishermen hold behind one short, broad woman.
Geum is fifty-two, both arms her own, with no Association to call. Just a boat's steel door and a terrified crew.
Then a young man walks out against the crowd, five fighters of light ahead of him and something vast with a lantern swimming alongside.
They dive into the sea one after another, the great lantern last.
Geum is standing in front of her own crew. She can't imagine sending anyone ahead.
Then he kneels past her line, amber threads running into his chest. Every blow down there lands on him.
One by one the threads snap, and the blood stops. It looks like relief.
It isn't. Under the water his fighters go out like candles. Once he stops carrying them, nobody comes back.
He walks off the end of the breakwater into the sea, toward a column of violet light, and is gone.
Then the sea erupts. Something rises, too big to see the end of, the same lantern burning violet on its crest.
A hand as wide as a building comes down on her door. That's how Geum lost her arm.
By daylight, cranes lower stone and steel onto a ring of light three hundred metres wide: the lid now shearing its bolts.
Back in the present, she flexes her steel fingers. The Wall of Busan never really retired. She works nights.
Jaeha has never heard of anyone with a power like his. Now he has, and how it ended.
He looks at his trembling hands and draws the obvious lesson. Geum only knows what she saw.
She taps the ladle over his heart. That's what the four o'clock runs are for.
Wednesday morning, the tiny auntie comes running: violet light is leaking from the cold store.
Between the racks of frozen fish: a brand-new little gate, on nobody's books.
The big gate is cracking, she says, so little ones leak. The Association? Geum has a licence and a ladle.
Then the day's rule, the hardest she could pick: no carrying. His summons take their own hits.
Jaeha hesitates, then switches off his own skill for one gate.
Nib goes through first, as always.
Inside: a flooded Far Side shrine, knee-deep in sea water, something sitting on the dais.
Three summons flare into field form. Jaeha can still talk to them, but not share the pain.
The shrine stands up: the Reef Hermit, a four-metre crab wearing it as a shell, a bell clanging inside.
Its big claw slams Borro into a pillar and pins him there.
Every instinct screams at Jaeha to take the hit. Geum's steel hand clamps his shoulder. No.
Lyra looses a second arrow, soaked, furious and magnificent, and both bounce off the stone.
Nib slashes a leg, and the smaller claw flings him into a pillar, arm cut open.
He gets up bleeding and glares at Jaeha. He knows what his Operator wants to do.
For Jaeha, watching is worse than bleeding. Geum stays calm: going first was their choice, and nobody is dying.
Then Jaeha notices the crab tapping Borro's shell, while its own cramped shrine crumbles.
Out comes the notebook. The Hermit isn't fighting Borro. It's house-hunting.
So, silently through LINK, Borro receives the strangest order of his career.
Borro does his best to look like an empty house.
The Hermit hauls its soft body out to move in, and for an instant it's bare.
Jaeha barely moves his lips. Lyra only needs two words.
Her arrow goes straight through, and Nib drives both knives into the crack.
The Hermit bursts into ash, and its empty shrine topples into the water.
Borro pats his shell plates shut, deeply offended, and sets the record straight.
A new kind of boss pays extra: Route Alignment fills to a hundred percent.
The bar spills over: Operator level seven, six minutes of field form, and a fourth summon slot.
The core is worth two million won, and again there's only one button. Jaeha keeps count of that.
Jaeha bandages Nib's arm with a strip of towel. To a soldier, being trusted with his own hit is respect.
Geum's gold tooth comes out. Day three, and finally a lesson that isn't about his body.
Back at the tent, Geum pays her soldiers in fish cakes. Lyra audits the payroll.
That night Jaeha stands where that man stood, with a fourth slot open and a call he's been saving.
Geum stands beside him. She doesn't ask what the window says. She tells him to answer it.
He touches the tiny cyan mark, and it blooms open.
Inside the Call, he has one minute. Of all the rifts, one is lit: a broken signal tower, something fluffy on top.
Then two enormous black eyes pop up an inch from his face. Somebody has waited a very long time.
